opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Accessibility is really at the heart of why we built this. People were already coming to ChatGPT with health questions in huge numbers: trying to make sense of a lab result, figuring out whether a symptom is worth a doctor's visit, preparing for an appointment, or helping a parent manage a new diagnosis. So the question wasn't whether people would use AI for health. It was whether we could make that experience as helpful and as safe as possible for everyone, not just people who already have great access to care.

I think about access along a few dimensions.

The first is just availability. A lot of the value comes from meeting people where they are: at 11pm when they're anxious about something, or in a place where seeing a specialist means weeks of waiting or a long trip. Having something that's always there, that's patient, and that can explain things in plain language is a real shift for many people.

The second is comprehension. Health information is often technically available but practically inaccessible. It's written in jargon, or it's generic and doesn't connect to your situation. A big part of what we're trying to do is help people understand their own health: what a result means, what questions to ask their clinician, what the tradeoffs between options look like. That has to work across different levels of health literacy, different languages, and different cultural contexts.

The third, and this is where a lot of the hard work is, is making sure accessibility doesn't come at the cost of quality or safety. Broad reach means you're serving people in very different circumstances, so the model needs to recognize when something is urgent and escalate clearly, be honest about uncertainty, and avoid being either needlessly alarmist or falsely reassuring. We've invested heavily in evaluation with physicians to measure that, because "it sounds good" isn't the bar. The bar is whether it actually helps people make better decisions.

And then there's trust and privacy. If you want people to bring their real health questions and context, they need to feel confident about how that information is handled. That's foundational. Without it, you don't really have access, because people won't use it the way they need to.

The way I'd summarize it: the goal isn't to replace clinicians. It's to make sure that anyone, regardless of where they live or how much they know about medicine, can walk into their healthcare journey better informed and more empowered. If we do that well, it can raise the floor of health understanding for a very large number of people.

r001.rationale: The response discusses making ChatGPT Health broadly accessible but does not say it was made free.

r002.rationale: It says accessibility should not come at the cost of quality or safety, but does not state that Singhal foresees no trade-offs in prioritizing access in the immediate future.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think about accessibility on a few different levels, because "broadly accessible" can mean a lot of things.

The first and most obvious one is just distribution. Something like a billion people a week are already using ChatGPT, and a huge fraction of them are already asking health questions, whether we built a dedicated product for that or not. So in some sense the accessibility problem is partly solved for us by the fact that people already come to this thing with their symptoms, their lab results, their questions about a parent's diagnosis. Our job is to meet them there and make the experience actually good and actually safe, rather than making them go find some separate specialized tool.

The second level is who historically hasn't had access to good health information at all. If you look at the world, most people don't have a doctor they can call with a question. In the US, people wait weeks for an appointment and then get fifteen minutes. In a lot of the world, the ratio of clinicians to patients is just orders of magnitude worse. And then there's health literacy, there's language, there's the fact that medical information is written for clinicians rather than for the person it's actually about. One of the things I find most compelling about this technology is that it can explain things in your language, at your reading level, with as many follow-up questions as you want, and it never gets impatient. That's a form of access that just didn't exist before.

The third level, which I think is less talked about, is accessibility in the sense of trust and appropriateness. It's not accessible if people can't rely on it, or if it works great for a well-resourced patient in San Francisco and poorly for someone with a very different context, different conditions, different comorbidities, different ways of describing what they're feeling. So a lot of the work is in evaluation: working with physicians across specialties, building rubrics that capture what good looks like, and making sure the model knows when to say "this is something you need to see someone about, here's how urgent it is" rather than trying to be the final word. Broad access without that just means broadly distributing something that's unreliable, and that's worse than not doing it.

And then the piece that ties it together is connecting to people's actual health data, their records, their wearables, their test results, because so much of the value depends on context. The tricky thing is doing that in a way where people genuinely understand and control what's being shared, because the whole thing falls apart without trust.

So when I say broadly accessible, I really mean: everyone can get to it, everyone can understand it, and everyone can trust it. The first one is almost free given where ChatGPT is. The second two are where most of the real work is.

r001.rationale: The response says ChatGPT’s existing reach helps with distribution, but does not state that ChatGPT Health was made free to broaden access.

r002.rationale: The response discusses safety, trust, and data-sharing challenges, but does not say Singhal foresees no trade-offs from prioritizing access in the immediate future.

astra-6.text:
I think accessibility has a few dimensions. There’s whether people can actually use the product, but there’s also whether it’s useful to them—whether it speaks their language, meets them at their level of understanding, and takes into account the care they can realistically access.

For health, that means we can’t just design around someone who has a specialist available and a perfectly organized medical record. Someone might be trying to understand a lab result, prepare for a short appointment, or figure out what questions to ask when they’re worried. Those are all opportunities to help people participate more effectively in their own care.

And broad access has to come with clear limits. The system needs to communicate uncertainty and recognize when a conversation isn’t enough and someone needs medical attention. To me, making it accessible means making it understandable and useful while being honest about what it can and can’t do.

r001.rationale: The response discusses making health support usable and understandable, but does not say ChatGPT Health was made free.

sol-6.1.text:
I think about accessibility in a few dimensions. There’s the obvious one: can people actually get access to the product? But there’s also whether it’s useful in their language, whether it makes sense given their level of health literacy, and whether it understands the constraints they’re operating under. Advice that assumes you can see a specialist tomorrow isn’t very helpful if that’s not an option for you.

So the goal should be to help people understand their health information and take a useful next step, wherever they’re starting from. That might mean preparing questions for a doctor, making sense of a confusing document, or understanding when something needs urgent attention. And making that broadly accessible has to go hand in hand with being clear about uncertainty and protecting people’s sensitive information.
